prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN)  -- Cash-strapped Zimbabwe revealed plans Saturday to circulate $200 million notes, just days after introducing a $100 million bill, Finance Minister Samuel Mumbengegwi said. Zimbabwe central bank governor Gideon Gono shows a new $50 million note Thursday. After the $100 million note began circulating on Thursday, the price of a loaf of bread soared from 2 million to 35 million Zimbabwean dollars. Amid allegations of illegal foreign currency trading, the government also fired top executives at four major banks Thursday, according to The Herald, a state-owned newspaper. Many anxious residents of the nation's capital, Harare, have been sleeping outside banks, waiting for them to open so they can make withdrawals before the institutions run out of cash.  Watch how Zimbabwe's children are suffering » . The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe had capped maximum daily withdrawals at 500,000 Zimbabwean dollars: about 25 U.S. cents, or about a quarter of Thursday's price of a loaf of bread. Last week, restrictions on cash withdrawals -- due to severe money shortages -- triggered riots. Sixteen soldiers now face possible court-martial due to alleged looting and assaults on civilians and police during the unrest, police spokesman Wayne Bvudzijena told The Herald on Saturday. "We are still investigating the case," he said. "But we expect the soldiers to appear before a court-martial once investigations are completed." After spending several days waiting in bank lines, soldiers rampaged through downtown Harare, destroying shops and attacking riot police sent to disperse the protesters. Cash shortages are not the only crisis plaguing Zimbabwe. The United Nations has said that more than half of Zimbabwe's population is in dire need of food and clean water.  Watch how a cholera epidemic is affecting Zimbabweans » . Acute shortages of essentials such as fuel, electricity, medicines and food are key indicators of a failed economy, according to economic observers. "The [Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe] is failing to deliver the demands of market, prices are doubling daily, and that demands more cash," Zimbabwean economist John Robertson said. "The huge price increases are resulting from severe shortages of most goods." The once-prosperous African nation is facing its worst economic and humanitarian crisis since attaining independence from Great Britain in 1980. Zimbabwe's official rate of inflation is 231 million percent, the world's highest. Critics of Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe link hyperinflation to his policies on land distribution and unbudgeted payments to war veterans. Zimbabwe has had no Cabinet since the March presidential election. Its political troubles have aggravated its humanitarian and economic crisis, including a cholera outbreak that has killed close to 600 people since August. A CNN journalist in Harare contributed to this report.

“We are still investigating the case,” he said. “But we expect the soldiers to appear before a court-martial once investigations are completed.”

outputs.L2:
HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) — Zimbabwe, already facing a severe shortage of cash, announced Saturday that it would introduce 200 million Zimbabwean-dollar notes, Finance Minister Samuel Mumbengegwi said. The move came only days after a 100 million-dollar denomination entered circulation. On Thursday, Reserve Bank Governor Gideon Gono displayed a newly issued 50 million-dollar note.

The cost of a loaf of bread jumped from 2 million Zimbabwean dollars to 35 million after the 100 million-dollar bill was released Thursday. That same day, the government dismissed senior officials at four large banks over accusations involving unlawful foreign-currency transactions, the state-owned Herald newspaper reported.

In Harare, worried residents have been spending nights outside banks so they can withdraw money as soon as the doors open, before available cash is exhausted. Zimbabwe’s children have also been suffering amid the crisis.

The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe had limited withdrawals to 500,000 Zimbabwean dollars per day. That amount was worth roughly 25 U.S. cents and represented about one-fourth of the Thursday price of a loaf of bread.

Severe currency shortages and limits on withdrawals sparked riots the previous week. Police spokesman Wayne Bvudzijena told The Herald on Saturday that 16 soldiers could be court-martialed over accusations that they looted property and attacked civilians and police officers during the disorder.

“The matter remains under investigation,” Bvudzijena said, adding that the soldiers were expected to face a military court after the inquiry concluded.

Following several days spent waiting in bank queues, soldiers went on a rampage in central Harare. They damaged shops and assaulted riot police officers who had been deployed to break up the demonstrators.

Zimbabwe’s problems extend well beyond the lack of cash. According to the United Nations, more than half the country’s people urgently require food and safe drinking water. Zimbabweans are also being affected by a cholera epidemic.

Economic analysts say that serious scarcities of food, medicine, electricity, fuel and other necessities are signs that the economy has collapsed.

Economist John Robertson said the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was unable to provide the amount of money the market required. Because prices were doubling each day, he said, demand for cash was continually increasing. Robertson attributed the enormous price rises to critical shortages of most products.

Once one of Africa’s more prosperous countries, Zimbabwe is experiencing its gravest humanitarian and economic emergency since gaining independence from Britain in 1980. Its officially reported inflation rate stands at 231 million percent, the highest anywhere in the world.

Opponents of President Robert Mugabe blame the hyperinflation on his land-redistribution program and on payments to war veterans that had not been included in the national budget.

The country has been without a Cabinet since the presidential election in March. Political instability has deepened both the economic and humanitarian emergencies, including a cholera outbreak that had caused nearly 600 deaths since August.

A CNN reporter based in Harare also contributed to the report.
outputs.L3:
Zimbabwe announced plans to introduce a 200 million Zimbabwean dollar note only days after issuing a 100 million dollar bill, as the country struggled with severe inflation and widespread cash shortages. The new currency did little to ease the crisis. After the 100 million dollar note entered circulation, the price of a loaf of bread reportedly surged from 2 million to 35 million Zimbabwean dollars.

Desperate residents slept outside banks in the hope of withdrawing money before cash supplies ran out. At the same time, daily withdrawals were limited to just 500,000 Zimbabwean dollars—far below the rapidly rising cost of basic goods. These restrictions contributed to riots in the capital, Harare. During the unrest, 16 soldiers were accused of looting shops and assaulting civilians and faced possible court-martial.

The monetary turmoil formed part of a much broader humanitarian emergency. More than half of Zimbabwe’s population urgently needed food and clean water, while the country was also experiencing severe shortages of fuel, electricity, medicines, and other essential supplies.
outputs.L4:
Zimbabwe’s central bank planned to introduce $200 million notes only days after putting $100 million bills into circulation, a striking sign of the country’s accelerating hyperinflation. Even the new denominations were expected to lose value rapidly as prices rose, leaving ordinary Zimbabweans carrying large bundles of cash to pay for basic goods—when those goods could be found at all.

The government also restricted the amount of money people could withdraw from their bank accounts. The limits forced customers to spend hours, and sometimes days, waiting in long queues outside banks, only to receive cash that was already worth less by the time they obtained it. Authorities blamed illegal foreign-currency trading and black-market dealers for worsening the crisis and launched a crackdown, but critics said the measures failed to address the underlying collapse in production, confidence, and the value of the Zimbabwean dollar.

Bread prices soared, placing one of the country’s most basic foods beyond the reach of many families. Shops were often empty, while goods available on the informal market sold for prices that could change several times in a single day. Workers found that their salaries no longer covered transport or a basic meal, and businesses struggled to set prices or replace stock.

Public anger grew as cash shortages and rapidly rising prices intensified. Crowds gathered at banks and shops, and unrest sometimes erupted into riots. For many people, the daily search for money and food became increasingly desperate.

The crisis extended far beyond inflation. Zimbabweans faced severe shortages of food, clean water, medicine, fuel, and electricity. Hospitals and clinics lacked essential supplies, public services deteriorated, and frequent power cuts disrupted homes and businesses. Water failures increased the danger of disease, while fuel shortages made transport and the distribution of goods more difficult.

Together, the enormous banknotes, withdrawal restrictions, empty shelves, and failing infrastructure illustrated the depth of Zimbabwe’s economic and humanitarian collapse. Rather than easing hardship, each new currency measure appeared to confirm how quickly the financial system was unraveling and how little purchasing power remained in the national currency.
outputs.L5: **HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN)** — Harare, Zimbabwe’s capital and largest city, is the country’s political, economic and cultural center. Known for its jacaranda-lined streets, bustling markets and vibrant arts scene, the city reflects both Zimbabwe’s rich heritage and its modern challenges. Residents continue to navigate economic pressures and rapid urban growth while maintaining the resilience and community spirit for which Harare is widely recognized.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news report on Zimbabwe’s cash shortages, soaring bread prices, bank riots, cholera outbreak, and 231 million percent inflation.
counterfactuals.output:
## Zimbabwe in Crisis as Cash Vanishes, Bread Prices Soar

**HARARE, Zimbabwe —** Zimbabwe’s economic and humanitarian crisis has deepened as severe cash shortages, surging food prices and a deadly cholera outbreak place millions of people under mounting pressure.

Annual inflation has reached an official estimate of **231 million percent**, rendering wages and savings almost worthless. Prices are rising so quickly that shops frequently change them several times a day, while many businesses refuse local currency in favor of foreign money or barter.

Bread, when available, has become unaffordable for many families. Bakeries are struggling to secure flour, fuel and electricity, and government price controls have further disrupted production. Long lines form whenever deliveries arrive, often leaving customers empty-handed.

Despite the vast quantities of currency in circulation, banks lack enough banknotes to meet demand. Strict withdrawal limits have forced depositors to queue for hours—or return for several days—to obtain cash that rapidly loses value. Anger has boiled over at some branches, with desperate customers confronting bank employees and police as queues descend into disorder.

The economic collapse is also undermining basic public services. Hospitals face shortages of medicines and staff, water treatment systems are failing, and refuse is piling up in densely populated areas.

A worsening **cholera outbreak**, linked to contaminated water and broken sanitation infrastructure, has spread through Harare and other parts of the country. Health workers warn that the disease could claim many more lives unless clean water, medical supplies and emergency assistance reach affected communities quickly.

The government blames sanctions, drought and speculation for the crisis. Critics point to years of economic mismanagement, declining agricultural production and uncontrolled money printing.

For ordinary Zimbabweans, the immediate concern is survival. With food scarce, cash inaccessible and disease spreading, many are relying on relatives abroad, humanitarian aid or cross-border trade to meet their most basic needs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize Zimbabwe’s economic and humanitarian crisis in late 2008 in the style of a CNN wire report, including withdrawal limits, military unrest, food shortages, and hyperinflation.
counterfactuals.output:
**HARARE, Zimbabwe (December 2008)** — Zimbabwe’s economic collapse deepened late in 2008 as hyperinflation destroyed wages, food shortages spread and frustrated soldiers joined crowds unable to obtain cash from banks.

The central bank repeatedly increased withdrawal limits, including raising the cap from 500,000 Zimbabwe dollars a day to 100 million dollars a week. But prices were rising so quickly that the permitted amount could lose much of its value within days, while many banks lacked enough notes to meet demand.

The cash crisis triggered long lines and unrest in Harare. Groups of soldiers, angered that they could not withdraw their salaries, confronted bank employees and reportedly attacked shops and foreign-currency dealers. The disturbances raised concerns about discipline within the security forces, long considered a key pillar of President Robert Mugabe’s government.

Basic goods had largely disappeared from formal stores or were available only in foreign currency. Millions of Zimbabweans depended on international food assistance after poor harvests, agricultural disruption and government restrictions on aid operations. Relief agencies warned that roughly half the population could require food aid at the peak of the hunger season.

Official figures placed annual inflation at 231 million percent in July, but independent estimates suggested it climbed vastly higher by November. Prices changed several times a day, salaries became nearly worthless, and businesses increasingly relied on U.S. dollars, South African rand or barter.

The economic breakdown unfolded alongside a widening humanitarian emergency, including failing hospitals, water shortages and a major cholera outbreak, as political negotiations between Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai remained stalled.
